<strong>La regla.</strong> Con taps en $: The rule. With taps at $x^1$ and $x^0$, the new bit is $s_{n-2} \oplus s_{n-1}$: the XOR of the two right-hand bits. At each step, the right-hand one goes out, everything shifts, and the new one comes in on the left.
<strong>La salida.</strong> 0, 0, 1, 0,: The output. 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, and back to the start. Any window of 3 consecutive bits appears exactly once in the period: it is the mark of a maximal-period LFSR.
<strong>Los pasos.</strong> 100 → sale 0: The steps. 100 → 0 out, $0 \oplus 0 = 0$ in: 010. → 0 out, $1 \oplus 0 = 1$ in: 101. → 1 out, $0 \oplus 1 = 1$ in: 110. → 0 out, $1 \oplus 0 = 1$ in: 111. → 1 out, $1 \oplus 1 = 0$ in: 011. → 1 out, $1 \oplus 1 = 0$ in: 001.
<strong>Uno más y se cierra.</strong> 00: One more and it closes. 001 → 1 out, $0 \oplus 1 = 1$ in: 100, the initial state. Seven states, all the non-zero ones: period $2^3 - 1 = 7$. The polynomial is primitive.

Alice and Bob share the short key, start the same register and get the same stream. So as never to repeat the stream between two messages, a number that changes with each message is added to the key, the nonce, which travels in the clear and is not secret: it only has to not repeat.

La idea es tentadora: si la clave no pue: The idea is tempting: if the key cannot be as long as the message, let a machine stretch it. You start from a short key, generate with it a stream of bits that looks random, the keystream, and XOR it with the message, as in Vernam. It is the stream cipher. It loses Shannon's perfection, because a deterministic machine does not produce randomness, but if the stream is unpredictable for Eve, the cipher holds.

Los LFSR están en el GPS: cada satélite: LFSRs are in GPS: each satellite emits a 1023-bit sequence generated by two 10-bit registers, and the receiver recognises it to measure the time of flight. Also in mobile telephony, in Bluetooth and in broadcasters' spreading codes, always to synchronise or spread, not to hide. When they have been used to encipher, things have gone badly: the A5/1 of GSM mobiles, three combined LFSRs, breaks in seconds, and the WEP encryption of the first wifi networks, based on RC4 with short nonces, broke in minutes and forced every network in the world to change.

The register has $2^n$ states, and the all-zeros state stays put for ever, so the period is at most $2^n - 1$. Solomon Golomb estudió las secuencias de: Solomon Golomb studied shift-register sequences in the nineteen-fifties and published the reference book in 1967. Elwyn Berlekamp gave in 1968 an algorithm for decoding certain codes and James Massey observed in 1969 that it was exactly what was needed to reconstruct the shortest LFSR that produces a sequence. Ron Rivest designed RC4 in 1987, a trade secret until somebody published it anonymously in 1994; Daniel Bernstein presented ChaCha in 2008, and today it protects a good part of internet traffic along with AES.

Since each new bit is a linear combination of the previous ones, if Eve knows $2n$ consecutive bits of the stream, she has a system of $n$ linear equations modulo 2 with $n$ unknowns, the taps, and she solves it. And she knows bits of the stream as soon as she knows a piece of the message: a header, a greeting, a format. Berlekamp and Massey's algorithm does all this in an instant.
